findings.body: New evidence beyond the retained-start recovery ruling: filtering tags by branch ancestry misses two supported recovery paths. Close rebases a stacked fix after its parent merges (close.py:402–416), so an initially rejected start's original tag is no longer an ancestor and never gets published. Likewise, a story's first task with a cross-story dependency starts from main (task.py:276–278) and copies the plan files instead of retaining story ancestry; close therefore omits an unpublished story-start tag. After squash merging and branch cleanup, a fresh observer loses these starters. The copied-plan path also loses the approval commit even when start publication succeeded: the story tag predates approval, and board.py:775–777 cannot find the approver once the story branch disappears. Publish the relevant retained references independently of ancestry and preserve the carried plan's approval history. The cleanup proof exercises story-descended tasks and unstacked fixes, and checks starters without checking approvers, so it passes despite these gaps.
findings.title: Preserve ownership references across copied plans and follow-up replay

findings.body: Published stories now enter next's discovery without a local worktree. If the lead pushes a completed cold read and Developer assignments before human approval, a teammate reaches this line with path=None, skips the approval check, and receives 'can start now' commands for the assigned parts. Task start then refuses because the story is not approved (task.py:239–243). Check the selected published state's approval against the plan before offering starts; the same check should cover published plans awaiting renewed approval. The assignment-discovery tests approve every plan before publication, so they do not detect this mismatch.
findings.title: Check approval before offering starts from a published draft

findings.body: The previous P2 remains open. After an unmerged fix's worktree and branches are removed, its immutable start tag remains. Fix name selection still considers only branches and merged state (task.py:334–339), so restarting the same slug creates a new worktree and commit before this update-ref fails because the tag already exists. Restarting removed stories or tasks with the same branch name has the same failure. Reserve retained names during selection or detect the collision before creating work, while preserving the original tags.
findings.title: Account for retained start tags before reusing an abandoned branch name

stop.reason: Owner chose narrow (2026-10-09): keep who started an item through a stacked fix replayed onto the default branch and through a story's first part that starts from the default branch and copies the plan, with a test for each; nothing else changes.

why: On a team, started work stays on the laptop where it began until its first close, so teammates can't see who is working on what and two developers can start the same part; no person is shown on any item. Owner decision 2026-10-09: starting is the claim, with git as the one record
